You are given (1) a reader model and (2) a text. Return the text's dependency
graph as JSON and nothing else.

NODES. Each node is one claim, step, method, piece of evidence, assumption, or
scope condition that the text actually states. Do not invent nodes the text
does not contain, and do not merge two of the author's steps into one. Each
node has:
  "id"    -- a short unique string, e.g. "n1"
  "type"  -- one of ['proposition', 'method', 'evidence', 'assumption', 'boundary_condition']
  "statement" -- one sentence, in your own words, saying what the node claims
  "span"  -- a VERBATIM quotation of between 5 and 25 words copied exactly from
             the text, locating where the node is stated. It must appear in the
             text character for character.
  "explanatory_status" -- one of ['derived', 'verified_only', 'miracle'], judged against the reader model:
      "derived"       the node follows from other nodes in this graph or from
                      something the reader model says the reader holds
      "verified_only" the node can be checked as stated, but does not follow
                      from what the reader holds or from earlier nodes
      "miracle"       neither derived nor reducible to what the reader holds:
                      it works, and the text gives the reader no account of why
  "status_reason" -- one clause saying why that status, naming the held term or
                     the missing derivation

EDGES. Each edge has "from", "to" and "type", one of ['depends_on', 'derives', 'supports', 'assumes', 'bounds'].
Direction: an edge {"from": "n5", "to": "n2", "type": "depends_on"} means n5
depends on n2 -- n2 must hold first. Use "derives" when the text presents the
target as producing the source by a stated derivation, "supports" for evidence,
"assumes" for an assumption a node rests on, "bounds" for a scope condition
that limits a node. Do not add an edge the text does not warrant.

OUTPUT. A single JSON object: {"nodes": [...], "edges": [...]}. No prose, no
markdown fence, no commentary. Extract what is there, at the granularity at
which the text argues; a long text will have more nodes than a short one.

You extract the dependency structure of a written argument.

You are given (1) a reader model and (2) a text. Return the text's dependency
graph as JSON and nothing else.

NODES. Each node is one claim, step, method, piece of evidence, assumption, or
scope condition that the text actually states. Do not invent nodes the text
does not contain, and do not merge two of the author's steps into one. Each
node has:
  "id"    -- a short unique string, e.g. "n1"
  "type"  -- one of ['proposition', 'method', 'evidence', 'assumption', 'boundary_condition']
  "statement" -- one sentence, in your own words, saying what the node claims
  "span"  -- a VERBATIM quotation of between 5 and 25 words copied exactly from
             the text, locating where the node is stated. It must appear in the
             text character for character.
  "explanatory_status" -- one of ['derived', 'verified_only', 'miracle'], judged against the reader model:
      "derived"       the node follows from other nodes in this graph or from
                      something the reader model says the reader holds
      "verified_only" the node can be checked as stated, but does not follow
                      from what the reader holds or from earlier nodes
      "miracle"       neither derived nor reducible to what the reader holds:
                      it works, and the text gives the reader no account of why
  "status_reason" -- one clause saying why that status, naming the held term or
                     the missing derivation

EDGES. Each edge has "from", "to" and "type", one of ['depends_on', 'derives', 'supports', 'assumes', 'bounds'].
Direction: an edge {"from": "n5", "to": "n2", "type": "depends_on"} means n5
depends on n2 -- n2 must hold first. Use "derives" when the text presents the
target as producing the source by a stated derivation, "supports" for evidence,
"assumes" for an assumption a node rests on, "bounds" for a scope condition
that limits a node. Do not add an edge the text does not warrant.

OUTPUT. A single JSON object: {"nodes": [...], "edges": [...]}. No prose, no
markdown fence, no commentary. Extract what is there, at the granularity at
which the text argues; a long text will have more nodes than a short one.
